runs.text: prida como pao, oßo, eſpada, &c. queſe que

lines.note: Continues the preceding page’s description of a long object, such as a stick, bone, or sword, broken across its middle. The initial prida completes the divided Portuguese comprida; the unhyphenated que at the right edge continues as bra below.

runs.text: bra pello meo, ou de traues.

lines.note: Completes quebra and specifies breaking through the middle or crosswise. The scan shows pello with two l types; the historical spelling is retained.
Uchioroshi is referred to the entry Voroxi, the verb oroshi/orosu, for lowering or bringing down. Vide is the italic cross-reference instruction, while the Japanese principal forms remain roman.

Uchiosame means pacifying or bringing under control; the next row specifies a kingdom subdued by warfare. The scan supports long ſ in the Japanese headword and the printed Portuguese Aqietar, without supplying the modern-looking u of aquietar.

runs.text: guar como reino, &c. por armas, ou cõ guerra.

lines.note: Completes apaziguar and describes pacifying a kingdom by arms or war. The abbreviating tilde in cõ remains unexpanded.
Uchiotoshi is knocking down or cutting away by a blow. The Portuguese explanation begins with derrubar com pancadas and continues on the following row.

runs.text: ou cortar cerce como ramo, mẽbro, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Adds cutting a branch or limb clean through. The final Vt introduces the arm-cutting example and is italic with the explanatory apparatus.
Kaina wo zundo uchiotosu describes cutting an arm clean off. The Portuguese bra at the line end continues as ço below; no absent hyphen is supplied.
Completes braço and then begins the separate example taka wo uchiotosu. The Portuguese To is continued by mar on the next row, defining the taking of a wild falcon.
Completes tomar algum falcão bravo, the falcon-taking sense of uchiotosu. This short continuation is retained as its own physical row.

runs.text: Couſa com que ſe cobre outra, co-

lines.note: Uchiooi is a covering placed over another object. The headword shows no secure accent over its o; the circumflex in the following verb’s inflection is a separate occurrence.
The example is a cloth over a tomb or bier. The visible b in tumba corrects the OCR’s tumha without modernizing the Portuguese.
Uchiooi, with the principal forms uô and ôta, means covering from above. The two printed circumflexes are retained as shapes, independently of the preceding noun.

The example describes covering oneself above with a katabira in an unobtrusive fashion, as explained below. The conspicuous gap before final e is retained in vchivouô e. The context suggests vchivouôte, but only faint specks survive in the gap and no t stem or crossbar can be securely recovered; the damaged ending remains a nonblocking uncertainty.

runs.text: Cubrindo por cima com hũa Ca-

lines.note: Mon. is the citation label following the Japanese example. The Portuguese begins “covering above with a katabira”; Ca- is the first printed portion of the garment name continued on the next row.

runs.text: tabira de maneira que ninguem repare, ou co-

lines.note: Completes the divided garment name Catabira and explains that the covering is arranged so that nobody notices or pays attention. The final co- starts como on the next row.

runs.text: mo que não he couſa de importancia.

lines.note: Completes como and says the action is treated as something of no importance. This completes the same example rather than opening a new entry.
Uchishigure denotes rain falling in winter or autumn. The gloss’s temporal qualification continues below; the historical spelling Chouer is preserved.
Adds autumn to winter as the season for uchishigure. The capital O in Outono belongs to the printed Portuguese.
Uchishiki is an ornamental silk cloth or framed fabric. The next rows describe where it is spread in a devotional setting.

runs.text: ſe eſtende ſobre algum banco, ou degrao por

lines.note: The cloth is spread over a bench or step. The final por connects with reverence and ornament on the next row.

The purpose is reverence and decoration before a Fotoque, a Buddhist image or figure in the gloss’s terminology. Reuerencia corrects the damaged OCR reading; Fotoque is visibly roman within the italic Portuguese explanation.
A second sense begins: a small plate of crystal, silver, or similar material. Laminazinha is the diminutive printed in the Portuguese definition.

runs.text: que poem nos perfumadores, per a ſobre eſta la-

lines.note: The small plate is placed in incense burners so that material can be burned upon it. The scan supports perfumadores and nos; la- continues the noun lamina below.

runs.text: mina, ou folha queimar algũa aguila, ou ca-

lines.note: Completes lamina and explains burning aguila or calamba on the plate or sheet. The damaged but legible queimar replaces OCR queimnar, and algũa aguila replaces the garbled incense name; the printed tilde remains over u.
Completes calamba, the second aromatic material named in the incense-burning explanation. It is a continuation, not a separate Japanese headword.

Uchishiwore means withering, as leaves or flowers do. The headword is heavily abraded, particularly the o after u; Vchixiuore is the chosen reading from the residual strokes and gloss. The subsequently consulted NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho (version 202510, record 272a08; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html) supports its lexical identification, not this copy’s individual glyphs.
The withering applies to leaves and flowers, completing fo-lhas from the preceding row. No new entry begins on this short line.
Uchishizumari denotes everything becoming silent and still. The scan supports Vchixizzumari with the historical doubled z rather than OCR Vchiaizzumari.
Completes the preceding definition as being very quiet and calm. Both Portuguese adjectives belong to the same headword.
Uchishu denotes household servants or young attendants. The visible sequence is Vchixu, correcting the OCR’s Vchuxu; x supplies the Japanese sh sound.

runs.text: Frecha de ferro comprido pera arre-

lines.note: Uchiya is an iron projectile or dart thrown by hand with a cord. The headword is Vchiya, not OCR Vemiya, and the final arre- continues arremesar below.

runs.text: meſar cõ amão por hũ cordelzinho q̃ lhe atão.

lines.note: Completes the explanation of throwing the dart with the hand using a small cord tied to it. The printed abbreviated cõ and q̃ and the spelling arremeſar are retained.
Uchiyaburi means breaking or smashing forcibly. The past form is printed utta and is not normalized to a modern morphological expectation.
The breaking is done with force or by delivering a blow. The short continuation completes the physical-action definition.
Uchiyemi denotes rejoicing or smiling. The Portuguese pairs alegrar-se with surrir-se; its historical spelling is retained rather than modernized to sorrir.
Uchiyose is advancing upon or attacking with a body of men. The Portuguese acometer and abalroar introduce the military example below.
Shiro ye ninju wo uchiyosuru describes bringing troops against a fortress. The Japanese verb continues after the printed hyphen on the next physical row.

runs.text: Dar na fortaleza com gente, ou chegar

lines.note: Completes uchiyo-suru and translates it as attacking the fortress with men, or approaching it with them. The closing verb chegar is continued by perto below.

runs.text: perto com a gente pera dar.

lines.note: Completes the alternative explanation: bringing the troops close in order to attack. This remains part of the fortress example.
Uchuu is explained as tenchi no ai, the space between heaven and earth. The scan supports the missing i in Tenchino; the headword’s visible mark is a caron over u.
Completes terra and gives Ar, air, as the gloss for the intervening space. The final roman S. marks written usage.
This distinct Uchǔ means being in the rain, explained by ame no uchi. Its vowel is u with a caron, not the OCR’s o; the Portuguese estar construction continues below.
Completes estando chouendo, “while it is raining.” The final roman S. again identifies literary or written usage.

runs.text: O que està ſempre em caſa.

lines.note: Uchuudo is a person who stays at home. The caron over u is part of the printed headword, and the gloss is not restricted further than the source states.

runs.text: Idem. Tomaſe per homem q̃ não ſa-

lines.note: Uchuuto is given as equivalent to the preceding stay-at-home term. Its caron was omitted by OCR; the Portuguese then elaborates the person’s lack of worldly experience.

runs.text: be o que vai no mundo, nẽ ſae apublico, &c.

lines.note: Completes sabe and explains someone who does not know what goes on in the world and does not go out in public. The scan supports mundo, not OCR mando, and separates be from the following article o.

runs.text: Aruore aßi chamada, cuia raiz ſer-

lines.note: Ukogi is a tree whose root serves medicinally. The gloss continues below with further uses of its leaves and wood; no modern species identification is imposed.

runs.text: ue de mezinha, & as folhas de Ayemono, &

lines.note: The root serves as medicine and the leaves as Ayemono, a prepared or dressed food. Ayemono is a Japanese term embedded within the Portuguese explanation, not an independent example sentence.

runs.text: o pao ſerue pera fazer vinho cozido com elle.

lines.note: The wood is used in making wine boiled with it, completing the utilitarian description of ukogi. The Portuguese wording is retained without specifying a modern preparation.

runs.text: Vcqi. l, qiut. i, Qino tçumaru coto.

lines.note: Ukki, alternatively qiut, is explained by ki no tsumaru koto: constriction or blockage of one’s vital feelings. The Japanese alternate retains its checked final t, and the Portuguese gloss begins Aba-famento across the line break.

runs.text: famento, ou a perto do coração. ¶

lines.note: Completes abafamento and gives a tightness of the heart. The following example begins Vcqi-, repeating the headword rather than OCR Voqi-.
Completes Vcqi-uo sanzuru, with harasu as an alternative, meaning to relieve one’s constricted feelings. The Portuguese is Deſabafar, with long s rather than the OCR’s f.
Ude denotes the arms. Ude no hone wo misuru introduces the idiom of showing what one’s arm can do, translated on the next row.

runs.text: Moſtrar hum quanto pode com ſeu braço.

lines.note: The idiom is explained as showing how much strength one possesses in one’s arm. Hum, the indefinite subject “one,” replaces the OCR’s ham.
Udebone denotes the bones of the arm. The Portuguese Oßos uses the visible beta-like s ligature, which OCR had mistaken for b.
Udekubi is the wrist, literally glossed as the neck of the hand. The printed joined damão is retained.

runs.text: Hũs pòs aceſos que poem nos braços

lines.note: Udegoo names burning powders put on the arms. The damaged Portuguese word is aceſos, matching the burning described below; the caron in the Japanese headword is retained.
The practice is performed as penance or ostentation. The contiguous ostentação corrects the OCR’s spurious word break, and the following example repeats Vdegǒ-.

runs.text: Queimar os braços com estes pòs

lines.note: Completes Vdegǒ-uo taku, burning the arms with these powders. The Portuguese refers to the same powders introduced above.

runs.text: que vão ardendo por cima da carne.

lines.note: The powders keep burning on the surface of the flesh. This completes the physical description without adding a purpose beyond those stated in the source.

runs.text: Hũ cordão que tẽ a eſpada, ou Catana

lines.note: Udenuki is the cord attached to a sword or Catana. The vowel between n and q is abraded; the surviving lower strokes support u, with lexical confirmation from the supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho (version 202510, record 272b07; Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). Catana is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese definition.

runs.text: nos punhos q̃ ſe mete no braço pera lhenão cair.

lines.note: The cord at the sword’s hilt goes around the arm to prevent the weapon from falling. Punhos, no braço, and lhenão correct the OCR’s corrupted readings; the joined lhenão is retained as printed.
Udesaki is glossed as the hands. The example likewise reads Vdeſaqiga tçuyoi, with long ſ, and continues with its opposite on the next row.

runs.text: Homẽ forte, ou fraco das mãos.

lines.note: Youai hito completes the alternative “a person weak in the hands,” contrasted with strong. Fito has f, not long s; Homẽ carries an abbreviation mark, and fraco corrects OCR fraro.
Udewaza is work or a feat performed with the arm. The final Vdevazauo starts the object phrase of the illustrative Japanese sentence.

runs.text: Homem que faz façanhas, ou a-

lines.note: Suru hito completes the phrase for a person performing feats with the arms. The initial is lowercase ſ, not OCR capital F; the Portuguese continues with lifting weights.

runs.text: leuanta peſos, &c. com os braços, ou mãos.

lines.note: Completes aleuanta and describes lifting weights with the arms or hands. This completes the feats-of-strength example.

runs.text: O prouar as forças apertando as

lines.note: Udeoshi is a trial of strength by pressing or gripping the hands. The Portuguese begins the description of the contest and continues below.

runs.text: mãos, ou fazendo força a algũa mão, ou dedo

lines.note: The contest may involve applying force to a hand or finger. The printed tilde in algũa is retained without expansion.
The purpose is to twist or bend the hand or finger. The following Vdevo- begins the Japanese example continued on the next row.
Completes udeoshi wo suru, conducting this trial or exercise. The rest of the gloss explains the opposing claims made by the participants.

runs.text: apostando hum que lhe não ande mouer a mão,

lines.note: One participant wagers that the other will not move his hand. The visible text is que lhe não ande; the unusual joined ande is preserved rather than silently rewritten as a modern auxiliary construction.

runs.text: ou braço, & outro porfiando que lho ha de

lines.note: Adds the arm and the other participant’s insistence that he will move it. Porfiando, “insisting,” corrects OCR porfuando and continues into mouer below.
Completes the second participant’s claim to move the hand or arm by force. This short row closes the contest-of-strength definition.

runs.text: Hũa certa erua que ſe come, aqual em quã

lines.note: Udo is an edible plant, with different names given for its successive stages of growth. The printed aqual is kept joined; quã begins enquanto across the physical line break.

runs.text: to eſta dentro da terra ja com algum olho, ou go

lines.note: The first stage remains in the earth with an eye or bud emerging. Olho corrects OCR onho, and the final go is continued by mo below without supplying a hyphen.
Completes gomo and states that the plant at this stage is called Vdo. The Japanese name is a complete roman word; the OCR’s alternating italic fragments have been removed.

runs.text: fora da terra algum tanto, ſe chama

lines.note: Once the plant has emerged somewhat from the soil it is called Dojen. The name is embedded in the Portuguese explanation, and the next row gives its later-stage name.
When fully grown the same plant is called Xica. The gloss is a sequence of historical plant names rather than a reason to substitute modern botanical nomenclature.
Udomi is the lowing of an ox or cow, with u and ǒda as its principal forms. X. and B. are roman regional and low-register labels, not italic pieces of the preceding gloss.

runs.text: Certa laya de comer como pastas muito

lines.note: Udon is described as a kind of food made in very thin pasta-like pieces. The physical description continues on the next row.

runs.text: delgadas de maſa de trigo cozidas a maneira

lines.note: The pieces are of wheat dough, cooked in the manner described below. The historical spelling maſa is preserved as printed.
The comparison is with letria or Quirimugui. Quirimugui is a Japanese food name within the Portuguese explanation and remains in the locally printed typeface.
Udondoofu is tofu prepared for eating like udon. The Portuguese borrowing Tǒfus has a visible caron rather than the OCR’s tilde; the row ends with the complete pera, without a hyphen.
Completes the tofu definition with “to eat like Vdon.” Vdon is the embedded Japanese comparison term, not a new headword.
Udonge is a very rare flower. The headword’s o and the Portuguese Flor and rara are visible despite abrasion, correcting OCR Vdangue, Fhor, and rera.

runs.text: V, fi, cu, nǒ. Vrei, canaximi, curuximi,

lines.note: The adjective paradigm V, fi, cu, nǒ is followed by Japanese words for sorrow, distress, and suffering. The list continues with nayamu below; these are Japanese equivalents, not Portuguese-embedded terms for typeface marking.
Nayamu completes the Japanese explanation. The Portuguese supplies sadness, hardship, and affliction as the range of meanings.

Vfu is a court dignity, with Vfu and Safu illustrated as paired offices. The damaged f letters have been restored from their surviving strokes and the following ministerial titles; no vowel accents are supplied from detached or neighboring marks.
Udaijin and Sadaijin identify the ministers of the right and left. Sadaijin corrects OCR Saaijin; the Portuguese continues by explaining their positions.

runs.text: lugar à mão direita, & eſquerda do

lines.note: Their places are at the right and left of the Dairi. The Portuguese direita is complete, and Dairi is visibly roman within the italic explanation.

Ugachi means opening or excavating, as with water eroding earth. Enlargement and comparison with the clear tt in utta on c1-l034 support atta, with the second t worn down, rather than the OCR’s ata; this also agrees with the supplied NINJAL lexical checkpoint.

runs.text: agoa que choa, & caua a terra. ¶

lines.note: The example begins Hana wo after the explanation of water flowing and hollowing the earth. Choa is retained as the printed Portuguese form, and terra corrects OCR teria; the Japanese sentence continues on the next page.

zones.label: Catchword
zones.note: The catchword repeats the start of vgatçu on the following page; the Japanese example begins with Fanauo in the final body row.
